The Stanley Cup is ice hockey's most prestigious championship trophy, awarded annually to the winner of the National Hockey League playoff tournament. It was donated in 1892 by Canadian Governor General Lord Stanley of Preston. It is one of the oldest trophies in professional sports and has become an enduring symbol of hockey excellence and tradition.

The trophy was first awarded in 1893 and is named after Lord Stanley of Preston, who donated it to recognize excellence in Canada's national sport. The physical trophy consists of a bowl, called the Permanent Bowl, bands that are engraved with team names, and a base that travels to winning teams for celebration. Each player on the Stanley Cup-winning team gets one day with the trophy in the off-season to celebrate with family and in their hometown—a cherished tradition that has become part of hockey lore.

The Montreal Canadiens have won the Cup a record twenty-four times, including five consecutive championships from 1956 to 1960. The New York Islanders won four consecutive Stanley Cups from 1980 to 1983, a feat matched only by the Montreal Canadiens and the Edmonton Oilers. Wayne Gretzky and the Edmonton Oilers won four consecutive Stanley Cups in the nineteen-eighties, establishing themselves as the decade's dominant team.

The trophy itself bears the marks of its storied history. It is missing teeth from being bitten, it has dents from celebrations, and it bears scars that reflect its role as hockey's most celebrated championship artifact. To win the Cup today, teams must win best-of-seven playoff series against three opponents in the modern format, starting with the Wild Card rounds.
